newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wants controls on annual Medicaid spending.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wants controls on annual Medicaid spending.

text.p: President Clinton is looking to cap annual Medicaid spending as part of an overall plan to balance the budget by 2002, causing concern among some governors and Democratic lawmakers, government and health officials said Tuesday.

In its fiscal 1998 budget, to be sent to Congress next month, the White House wants to limit yearly increases in Medicaid, now an open-ended entitlement programme serving more than 35 million poor, elderly and disabled people, officials said.
The White House plan would allow per capita Medicaid spending to grow at about the same rate as the gross domestic product, Democratic congressional aides said.

They said the cap could save about $10 billion over five years from Medicaid, in addition to more than $50 billion in savings due to lower than expected growth in the programme. The White House expects more savings from cuts in payments to hospitals that serve a large number of indigent people.
The Medicaid proposal is just one part of major health care spending cuts that will be included in the budget blueprint Clinton sends to Congress.

Administration officials said earlier this week the budget would reduce spending for Medicare, which provides health coverage for elderly Americans, by $100 billion over five years. The cuts will come from reducing payments to doctors, hospitals and other health care providers.

"We do have an interest in making sure that in our Medicare and Medicaid proposals we generate sufficient savings that are consistent with the president's balanced budget goal," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry.
Part of the Medicaid savings could be ploughed back into a proposal to expand health coverage to uninsures children.
Some industry officials criticised the Medicaid plan, saying programme costs had already declined dramatically due to lower enrollment growth and state cost containment efforts.
They fear a cap could force states to cut services to vulnerable populations if growth was higher than expected.

Lynn Sagnani, vice president for the National Association of Public Hospitals and Health Systems, said it was too early to gauge the impact a broad new welfare law would have on the number of poor people eligible for Medicaid.

Medicaid is jointly funded by the state and federal governments. The programme grew an average of 22.4 percent a year between 1988 and 1992. Growth has slowed recently and was only 3.3 percent last year, the lowest rise in decades.
Administration officials noted Clinton's Medicaid plan is not new. He made similar proposals in the last session of Congress, as part of failed budget talks with Republicans.

Some Democratic governors and lawmakers grudgingly supported the cap at that time as an alternative to a far-reaching proposal by the Republicans to turn Medicaid into a block grant programme that states would run.

"Our governors endorsed that in the last Congress because they were looking at a block grant coming down the track," a Democratic Governors Association official said. "The situation seems to have changed some, so we're looking at it anew."
The federal government spent $86.3 billion on Medicaid in fiscal 1995, while states spent $65.3 billion, according to the Department of Health and Human Services.
